42867758.label: Background
42867758.text: There is an urgent need for clinical biomarkers to monitor the mechanistic efficacy of immunotherapy in oncology. The [18F]F-AraG tracer, developed to image activated T cells, may provide the means to establish such a biomarker. This study extends previously reported pharmacokinetic findings in untreated NSCLC across additional tumor types undergoing immunotherapy, and examines [18F]F-AraG kinetics in various organs. Four patients with advanced solid tumors were included in this phase 1 trial investigating a stimulator of interferon genes agonist with anti-programmed cell death protein 1. Patients underwent a 90 min [18F]F-AraG PET/CT scan at baseline, one week and six weeks on-treatment. The tracer kinetics in tumors and organs were modeled using three compartment models. Model selection was based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC), visual assessment of the fit quality, and the reliability of estimated kinetic parameters. The relationship between the primary kinetic measures (influx rate (Ki), volume of distribution (VT)) and the simplified uptake metrics (standardized uptake values (SUV), tumor-to-blood ratio (TBR) and tumor-to-plasma ratio (TPR)) were evaluated using scatter plots.

42867758.label: Results
42867758.text: The kinetics of all tumors and most organs were adequately described with the two-tissue irreversible model (2T3K), which was identified as the preferred model based on the AIC in 40/55 tumor regions. For most organs, the 2T3K model was selected. We observed a consistent linear trend across all metrics for the relationship between primary kinetic parameters and simplified uptake metrics. However, a patient-specific bias can be observed for SUV and TBR, which was corrected for when using the TPR.

42867758.label: Conclusion
42867758.text: This study confirms that [18F]F-AraG PET uptake in tumors is best described by a 2T3K model, with no treatment-induced effects observed. Quantification of [18F]F-AraG uptake in static scans is most reliable when normalized using the TPR.

42878808.text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.

42880958.text: Evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas derives mainly from small, single-center studies. The French national multicenter MELUTE study aimed to consolidate these data using a standardized regimen within a compassionate-use program approved by a national multidisciplinary tumor board. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, patients with refractory meningiomas treated with [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in 18 French centers between July 2022 and December 2024 were included. Treatment consisted of 7.4 GBq every 8 wk for up to 4 cycles. Clinical data (demographics, histologic World Health Organization grade [WHO], prior treatments, number of cycles, toxicity, progression, survival status as of October 1, 2025) were collected. Baseline [68Ga]Ga-DOTATOC PET and brain MRI scans obtained before and after treatment were centrally reviewed. The primary endpoint was 6-mo progression-free survival (PFS) assessed using volumetric Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Group criteria. Secondary endpoints were PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Sixty-nine patients were included (mean age, 65.1 ± 13.2 y; 52% female): 13 WHO grade 1, 42 WHO grade 2, 8 WHO grade 3, and 6 without histology. Most had prior surgery (86%) or radiotherapy (93%); 32% received prior systemic therapy. Twelve patients (17%) did not complete 4 cycles; only one discontinuation was toxicity-related. Six-month PFS was 70% (95% CI, 58.7-80.4%). Median PFS was 14.6 mo (95% CI, 13.3-18.5 mo), and median OS was 27.6 mo (95% CI, 24.2 mo to not reached). Grade 3 adverse events, mainly lymphopenia, occurred in 16%. Meningioma WHO grade independently predicted PFS, whereas higher Karnofsky performance status and corticosteroid use were protective; worse OS was associated with higher baseline tumor growth rate and prior systemic therapy. Conclusion: MELUTE demonstrates promising efficacy and favorable safety of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas with limited therapeutic options.

42957208.text: Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry, the current standard biomarker for predicting response to programmed death protein 1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer, has moderate predictive value among others because of tumor heterogeneity and limited biopsy representation, whereas PD-L1 PET/CT using 18F-BMS-986192 enables noninvasive, whole-tumor assessment of PD-L1 expression and heterogeneity, potentially improving prediction of response to immunotherapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter biomarker exploration study, patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer eligible for nivolumab-based therapies underwent baseline 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT, and tumor biopsy for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry before treatment initiation. The primary endpoint was durable clinical benefit, defined as progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 mo or greater, with secondary analyses assessing associations among tracer uptake, PD-L1 expression, survival outcomes, and PET-based radiomic features. Results: Of 91 enrolled patients, 77 were included in the final analysis of 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT. Although PD-L1 immunohistochemistry did not differ between patients with PFS of less than 9 mo versus 9 mo or greater, PD-L1 PET uptake in lung lesions was significantly higher in patients with PFS of at least 9 mo (P = 0.01). Using an optimal mean SUVpeak cutoff of 2.4, PD-L1 PET demonstrated a high negative predictive value (94%) for durable clinical benefit, with significant associations for both PFS and overall survival, particularly in patients receiving first-line treatment. Tracer uptake showed no correlation with 18F-FDG uptake. Conclusion: 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT revealed interpatient PD-L1 variability. Low uptake in lung lesions predicted poor outcomes with high negative predictive value. 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT demonstrated stronger negative predictive value than did baseline PD-L1 immunohistochemistry in this cohort. These findings require prospective validation.

42967258.label: Objective
42967258.text: To evaluate and compare the diagnostic performance of Node-RADS, dual-energy CT (DECT)-derived quantitative parameters, and their combination for distinguishing metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes (LNs) in patients with resectable gastric cancer (GC).

42967258.label: Materials and methods
42967258.text: Between Jan 2022 and Oct 2025, 115 consecutive patients with resectable GC who underwent preoperative triple-phase enhanced DECT scans and radical gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy were retrospectively enrolled. A total of 151 regional LNs (70 metastatic, 81 non-metastatic) with region-level pathological confirmation were selected for node-level comparison. Two radiologists independently assessed Node-RADS scores for each LN. LN short diameter (SD) was measured at the venous phase on the maximal axial slice. DECT-derived parameters (CT attenuation at 40 keV, iodine concentration (IC), and effective atomic number (Zeff) across arterial, venous, and delayed phases) were analyzed using a freehand region of interest on the maximal axial slice of the LN. Diagnostic performances were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis and compared using the DeLong test.

42967258.label: Results
42967258.text: IC at delayed phase (ICDP) was the sole parameter associated with LN involvement. The initial Node-RADS score (cut-off ≥ 3) achieved an AUC of 0.859 (95% CI: 0.793-0.910), significantly outperforming SD (AUC: 0.780, p < 0.05) and ICDP (AUC: 0.612, p < 0.05). Two modified Node-RADS algorithms incorporating ICDP under different rule-in and rule-out criteria were established, but did not improve diagnostic performance beyond the initial Node-RADS scores.

42967258.label: Conclusion
42967258.text: Node-RADS demonstrates superior diagnostic performance compared with DECT-derived quantitative parameters for identifying metastatic regional LNs in resectable GC, and can be reliably applied in the DECT settings.

42967258.label: Key points
42967258.text: Question Preoperative differentiation of metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes in resectable gastric cancer remains inaccurate using conventional size criteria. Findings Node-RADS (AUC = 0.859) outperformed SD diameter (continuous: AUC = 0.780; its > 8 mm dichotomized counterpart: AUC = 0.748) and ICDP (AUC = 0.612) for metastatic LN discrimination. Clinical relevance Node-RADS is a standardized and reproducible criterion that can be applied in dual-energy CT scenarios to effectively identify regional lymph node metastasis in resectable gastric cancer.

42969958.label: Background
42969958.text: The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) diagnostic algorithm assesses hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) probability of liver observations in high-risk individuals, but complexity may limit its adoption.

42969958.label: Purpose
42969958.text: To evaluate whether LI-RADS v2018 can be simplified without impairing diagnostic performance by removing threshold growth (TG) and reducing size cut-offs.

42969958.label: Population
42969958.text: Eight thousand five hundred eighty-two patients (mean age: 59 ± 11 years; 6610 male) at risk for HCC with CT/MRI (986 CT, 6554 MRI, and 1042 CT/MRI).

42969958.label: Field strength/sequence
42969958.text: Field strength: 1.5T and 3.0T; sequences varied by institution per LI-RADS technical requirements.

42969958.label: Assessment
42969958.text: LI-RADS v2018 using major features only was compared with seven simplifications removing TG and/or applying single size cut-offs (≥ 10, ≥ 15, and ≥ 20 mm) in individual participant data (IPD) of 64 studies (29 institutions, 11 countries) from the LI-RADS Living Systematic Review and IPD Meta-analysis Project. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2.

42969958.label: Statistical tests
42969958.text: Summary receiver operating characteristic curves estimated area under the curve (AUC) across LR-3 to LR-5; LR-5 sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) were estimated using a one-step bivariate mixed-effects model. Differences were assessed by cluster bootstrap. p < 0.05 indicated significance, uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

42969958.label: Results
42969958.text: Nine thousand four hundred six observations were included. Excluding TG with a 10-mm cut-off showed AUC similar to LI-RADS v2018 (0.80 vs. 0.81, p = 0.44) and significantly higher LR-5 sensitivity (73.8% vs. 71.8%) with similar specificity (72.5% vs. 73.7%, p = 0.13) and PPV (97.8% vs. 97.8%, p = 0.73). Removing TG with 15-mm and 20-mm cut-offs had significantly lower AUC than v2018 (-0.03 [95% CI: -0.041, -0.019]; -0.043 [-0.054, -0.032], respectively) and sensitivity (-13.2% [95% CI: -14.5%, -12.0%]; -30.1% [-31.7%, -28.5%], respectively). Of the 64 studies, 17 had low-risk of bias, and 56 had low applicability concerns.

42969958.label: Conclusion
42969958.text: Simplifying LI-RADS v2018 by removing TG and using a 10-mm size cut-off preserved diagnostic table AUC while improving LR-5 sensitivity without loss of specificity or PPV.

42975708.label: Objectives
42975708.text: To develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline that automates optimal circular region-of-interest (ROI) placement and the surrounding elastogram box, provides probe-angle/contact guidance, and measures skin-to-capsule distance (SCD) to standardize liver SWE acquisition, aiming to reduce operator-dependent variability.

42975708.label: Materials and methods
42975708.text: A two-stage pipeline combined SimCLR self-supervised pretraining on 17,441 unlabeled ultrasound images, followed by ENet fine-tuning using 495 annotated images for liver segmentation and 1564 images for poor probe contact detection. Segmentation outputs were combined with constraints on valid liver tissue pixels, axial depth, lateral boundaries, and regions of poor acoustic coupling to generate masks for optimal ROI placement. A distance transformation algorithm then identified optimal ROI coordinates within these masks. An inter-observer reader study assessed AI performance by comparing automated ROI placement, SCD measurements, and probe-angle correction guidance with annotations from expert attending radiologists.

42975708.label: Results
42975708.text: 18,182 US images from 654 liver elastography examinations in 609 patients (mean age, 52.6 ± 12.95 years; 55.4% male) were acquired from three ultrasound systems. The AI pipeline achieved liver segmentation performance with a Dice coefficient of 0.89, sensitivity of 0.95, specificity of 0.93, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94. The reader study demonstrated significantly higher AI-to-attending radiologist agreement (93.8%) compared to inter-attending agreement for ROI placement (81%). Cohen's kappa agreement between two attending radiologists was 0.25.

42975708.label: Conclusion
42975708.text: The proposed AI-driven pipeline significantly improved ROI placement consistency and reproducibility, highlighting its potential to enhance clinical reliability in liver fibrosis assessment.

42975708.label: Key points
42975708.text: Question Operator-dependent variability in region-of-interest (ROI) placement compromises measurement reproducibility in B-mode shear wave elastography. We developed an AI pipeline to place an optimal ROI. Findings The AI pipeline achieved liver segmentation performance of Dice 0.89 (AUC 0.94) and demonstrated higher AI-to-attending agreement (93.8%) than inter-attending agreement (81%) for ROI placement. Clinical relevance By standardizing ROI placement, elastogram box selection, and probe angle/contact guidance, the AI pipeline reduces operator-dependent variability in liver SWE acquisition, supporting more reproducible liver stiffness measurements that could improve fibrosis staging reliability.

42998158.label: Objective
42998158.text: The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT).

42998158.label: Materials and methods
42998158.text: This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis.

42998158.label: Results
42998158.text: Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897).

42998158.label: Conclusions
42998158.text: MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms.

42998158.label: Key points
42998158.text: Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.

43002608.text: An 80-year-old man with poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT for initial staging and treatment response assessment following pembrolizumab therapy. Follow-up PET/CT demonstrated a new FDG-avid focus within the T3 vertebral body without a corresponding CT abnormality. Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI revealed no structural correlate at the site of uptake. A repeat PET/CT performed 3 months later showed complete resolution of the vertebral lesion without additional treatment. The imaging findings favored transient immune-related inflammatory uptake or a pseudoprogression-like phenomenon rather than true osseous metastasis.
